report:
## Does Honey Help Acute Cough in Children?

**Conclusion: Likely yes, for children over 1 year old.** Multiple randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews suggest honey provides modest benefit for relieving acute cough symptoms and improving sleep quality in children with upper respiratory tract infections, though evidence quality varies.

**What the evidence shows:**

The Cochrane systematic review found that honey "probably relieves cough symptoms to a greater extent than no treatment, diphenhydramine, and placebo, but may make little or no difference compared to dextromethorphan." Honey also probably reduces cough duration better than placebo and salbutamol ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children)).

A more recent 2023 systematic review reinforced this, concluding there is "low quality evidence that honey may be more effective than cough medication or placebo/no treatment in relieving symptoms and improving sleep in children with acute cough," while calling for higher-quality blinded trials to confirm effectiveness ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10570220/)).

Comparative data suggest honey performs similarly to dextromethorphan (a common OTC cough suppressant) and may modestly outperform diphenhydramine, with mild side effects (nervousness, insomnia, hyperactivity) reported in some studies ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25404607/)).

**Important safety caveat:** Honey should never be given to infants under 12 months old due to the risk of infant botulism from Clostridium botulinum spores potentially present in honey — a risk unrelated to cough treatment but critical for any recommendation ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children)).

**Bottom line:** For children over age 1, honey appears to be a reasonably effective, low-risk, low-cost option for symptomatic relief of acute cough, comparable to or better than some OTC cough medications — though evidence remains of low-to-moderate quality and larger, well-designed trials are still needed.
